title: Among recent writers Louis of Dole, a Capuchin, follows Durandus (as reported by Rutherford)
source_text: II. Inter recentiores vero Ludovicus quidam a Dola ex ordine Capucinorum, cujus liber cum multis Doctorum approbationibus in lucem editus est, ad illam Durandi sententiam accedit. Dicit enim, Deum cum homine in agendo concurrere nihil aliud esse quam Vel liberum arbitrium creare, ut in actibus naturalibus, Vel dare in supernaturalibus potentiam, seu habitum agendi, per quam ipsa Voluntas totum faciat in omni actu supernaturali, absque ullo alio Dei concursu immediato actionem actu promovente. Prout hujus Viri Verba referuntur a Samuele Retorforti Theologiae Professore in Academia Andreapolitana Disputatione Scholastica de divina providentia cap. 25.
pass_a_gloss: But among the more recent a certain Louis of Dole of the order of Capuchins, whose book was put forth with many approbations of Doctors, accedes to that opinion of Durandus. For he says, that for God to concur with man in acting is nothing else than Either to create free choice, as in natural acts, Or to give in supernatural acts a power, or habit of acting, by which the Will itself does the whole in every supernatural act, without any other immediate concurrence of God actually promoting the action. As the Words of this Man are reported by Samuel Rutherford Professor of Theology in the University of St Andrews in the Scholastic Disputation on divine providence chap. 25.
pass_b_english: Among more recent writers, a certain Louis of Dole, of the Capuchin order, whose book appeared with many approvals from theologians, comes over to Durandus's view.

He says that God's concurring with man in action amounts to nothing more than creating free choice, in natural acts, or, in supernatural acts, giving a power or habit of acting by which the will itself does the entire work in every supernatural act, without any further immediate concurrence of God actually advancing the action. His words are reported in this form by Samuel Rutherford, professor of theology at the University of St Andrews, in his Scholastic Disputation on Divine Providence, chapter 25.

choices.why: The Schools' term for God's acting together with secondary causes; 'concurrence' keeps it recognizable as the technical term, with 'cooperation' kept for cooperatio.
